newsitem.title: USA: IBM raises dividend for second time in a year.
newsitem.headline: IBM raises dividend for second time in a year.

text.p: International Business Machines Corp. said Tuesday it will raise its dividend and expand its stock buyback programme, moving to return more of its stockpile of cash to investors.

The dividend increase, IBM's second in less than a year, brings the company's quarterly payout 5 cents to 40 cents a share, or 20 cents a share adjusted for a previously announced 2-for-1 stock split that was to be voted on Tuesday at the company's annual meeting.
IBM last raised its dividend in June 1996, when it lifted the payout 40 percent to a pre-split 35 cents a share.

The company, whose stock is one of the most widely held in the United States, said its board authorised an additional $3.5 billion in share repurchases, supplementing a budget that had dwindled to about $800 million after IBM's $2 billion in stock buybacks in the first quarter.

IBM stock jumped after the news of the moves, adding $5.625 to $156 in active trading on the New York Stock Exchange. It also got a boost from a rally in the broader market after the government reported economic news that encouraged investors.
Analysts had said before the meeting that the world's largest computer maker was likely to either raise the dividend or expand the stock buyback, though few thought it would do both.
The moves were the latest vote of confidence in its finances by the Armonk, N.Y.-based company, which had $6.4 billion in cash at the end of the first quarter.

When financial woes beset the behemoth in the early 1990s, IBM's peak annual dividend payout was $4.84 a share. Amid huge losses and layoffs, IBM slashed its dividend for the first time ever in January 1993.
After that the company brought in Louis Gerstner, who joined IBM after its search for a chief executive, in April 1993.

IBM's annual dividend, while still low relative to its stock price, is considered respectable for a technology company, since many high-tech firms do not pay cash dividends because they must invest heavily in research and development.
Since IBM's cash position is improving as it generates cash almost every quarter from operations, shareholders have said they wanted more returns.

In its first-quarter earnings, IBM was able to surpass most Wall Street estimates, despite a decline in mainframes, minicomputers and workstations, with the help of revenue growth in other faster growing, but lower profit businesses, a lower tax rate and fewer shares outstanding.
Its stock soared 8 percent on Thursday after it reported the better-than-expected earnings.
IBM's dividend is payable June 10 to shareholders of record on May 9.
